source: Pressure and Depth
In a still fluid P = P₀ + ρgh, and gauge pressure leaves out the air pressure above.
Students think a wider container makes the pressure at the bottom greater, when only the depth matters.

You know from Pressure that pressure is force spread over area, $P = F/A$, measured in pascals ($1\,\text{Pa} = 1\,\text{N/m}^2$), and from Density that density is mass per volume, $\rho = m/V$. Put the two together and you can find the pressure anywhere in a still liquid. It is why your ears hurt at the bottom of a pool and why a dam is thickest at its base.

Picture a column of water inside the lake, with cross-section $A$, reaching from the surface down to depth $h$. It is at rest, so by the first law the forces on it balance. The water below pushes it up with $PA$. The air above pushes it down with $P_0 A$, and its own weight pulls it down with $mg = \rho (Ah) g$. So $PA = P_0 A + \rho A h g$. Divide by $A$: $$P = P_0 + \rho g h.$$ The area cancelled. Only the depth matters, not how wide the water is.

In a still fluid, $P = P_0 + \rho g h$, where $P_0$ is the pressure at the surface (usually the air, about $1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$) and $h$ is the depth. The gauge pressure $P - P_0 = \rho g h$ leaves out the air. Pressure depends on depth, not on the shape of the container.
Four containers filled to the same depth. At any depth, all four gauges read the same $\rho g h$.
Two ways to report the same pressure.
Worked examples

Find the gauge pressure and the absolute pressure $3.0\,\text{m}$ below the surface of a swimming pool. Use $\rho = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $P_0 = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$.
Pressure in a pool
$2.94 \times 10^{4}\,\text{Pa}$ gauge; $1.30 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$ absolute
Gauge pressure: $\rho g h = (1000\,\text{kg/m}^3)(9.8\,\text{m/s}^2)(3.0\,\text{m}) = 29{,}400\,\text{Pa}$.
Units: $\text{kg/m}^3 \cdot \text{m/s}^2 \cdot \text{m} = (\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}^2)/\text{m}^2 = \text{N/m}^2 = \text{Pa}$.
Absolute pressure: $1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} + 0.294 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa} = 1.30 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$, about 1.3 times the air pressure.
How deep must you go in fresh water for the water alone to add one atmosphere, $1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$?
One more atmosphere
Set the gauge pressure equal to one atmosphere: $\rho g h = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}$.
So a diver at about $10\,\text{m}$ feels twice the surface pressure, and each further $10\,\text{m}$ adds about one more atmosphere.

A wide tank with a floor of $1.5\,\text{m}^2$ and a thin pipe with a floor of $0.010\,\text{m}^2$ are both filled with water to $2.0\,\text{m}$. Compare the gauge pressure and the force of the water on each floor.
Same depth, different floors
Equal pressures, $1.96 \times 10^{4}\,\text{Pa}$; forces $29{,}400\,\text{N}$ and $196\,\text{N}$
Pressure: both floors are $2.0\,\text{m}$ deep, so both feel $\rho g h = (1000)(9.8)(2.0) = 19{,}600\,\text{Pa}$.
Force on the tank's floor: $F = PA = (19{,}600\,\text{Pa})(1.5\,\text{m}^2) = 29{,}400\,\text{N}$.
Force on the pipe's floor: $(19{,}600\,\text{Pa})(0.010\,\text{m}^2) = 196\,\text{N}$. Same pressure, very different forces, because the areas differ.

Thinking a wider container, or one holding more water, has more pressure at the bottom. Pressure is force per area: the extra water in a wide tank rests on extra floor. In a container that flares out at the top, the slanted walls hold up the extra water; in one that narrows at the top, the walls push down on the water. Check: the formula $P = P_0 + \rho g h$ has no width in it. A second slip is mixing up gauge and absolute pressure; ask whether the air is included.
